title: Remarriage is allowed
hook: the code allows widows and widowers to remarry

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Anand Karaj: the lavan of Guru Ram Das, each sung as the couple walks around the Granth. Your line was four rounds. Which couple did you wish well? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-nine.

She wears white, or pale colors, and has for a long time. At family weddings she helps in the kitchen but keeps to the edge of the courtyard, away from the bride. Nobody says it to her face, but everybody knows what she is supposed to be now: finished. Her husband died, and in the eyes of the people around her, her own life ended with his. In the Punjab the Gurus knew, that was how a widow could be treated. In some places, worse was expected of her. Against that background, one short line in the Sikh code reads like a door being unlocked.
screen: `A WIDOW IN WHITE.` → `KEPT TO THE EDGE.` → `A DOOR BEING UNLOCKED.`

segments.voice: The Sikh Rehat Maryada says, in paraphrase: if a woman's husband has died, she may, if she wishes, marry again, to a suitable match. The same holds for a man whose wife has died. And the ceremony is the same Anand Karaj, the same four rounds. Look at the small words. If she wishes. The code doesn't push anyone into a second marriage, and it doesn't forbid one. The choice belongs to the person who is grieving. And the same ceremony. No lesser wedding, no quiet back-room version for someone who has been married before. She walks the same rounds around the same Guru. Now the background. The Gurus' world had a custom, sati, in which some widows burned on their husbands' funeral pyres. Guru Amar Das spoke against it. In a salok on Ang seven hundred eighty-seven, he says, in paraphrase, that those who burn with their husbands' bodies are not truly satis; true satis are those who live on in virtue and contentment, and who would die of the pain of separation alone. He takes a word that honored burning and gives it to the living. Tradition says Guru Amar Das also discouraged the veil and spoke for widows' dignity. The code carries that line forward. A spouse's death is a real ending, and the code doesn't pretend otherwise; Sikhs grieve, and the next lesson is about how. But the survivor is not ended with them. Their life still belongs to them, within the Guru's will, and they are allowed to start again.
screen: `A WIDOW OR WIDOWER MAY REMARRY.` · `IF SHE WISHES: THE CHOICE IS HERS.` · `THE SAME ANAND KARAJ.` · `GURU AMAR DAS AND THE LIVING.` · then, large: `STARTING OVER ALLOWED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: support someone starting over. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone beginning again: after a death, a divorce, a lost job, a move, an illness. Picture where they are right now. Then think of one plain thing that would help them. Not advice. Maybe an invitation, a meal, a message that says you're glad they're still in the picture. Hold them, and that one thing, until the bell. If you pray, you can remember them before Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Remarriage is allowed. The Sikh code lets a widow or widower marry again, if they wish, with the same Anand Karaj. Today's word.
Your line: starting over allowed. Today, do the one plain thing for the person you pictured, or for yourself, if you're the one beginning again. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: The Sikh Rehat Maryada permits a widow or widower to remarry if they wish, and such a marriage is solemnized with the same Anand Karaj ceremony as any other Sikh wedding.
